title: IB Geography Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
summary: IB Geography common mistakes cost avoidable marks. Learn to handle command terms, units, evidence and timing with a reliable exam-day routine.
body_markdown:
A student can know the geography and still lose the mark.


Imagine Maya, a hypothetical IB Geography student, opening her marked mock exam. She had revised urbanisation, climate vulnerability and global resource consumption. Her answers were full. Some were even impressive. Yet the marks disappeared in small, preventable ways: she described when asked to explain, copied a graph value without its unit, named a case study without using evidence and spent so long on an early response that her final essay became a hurried paragraph.


These are among the most important **IB Geography common mistakes** because they are not usually failures of knowledge. They are failures of execution. The solution is to treat every question as a precise task: decode the command term, identify the required evidence, protect the units and manage time according to the marks available.


### A quick Geography exam checklist


Before writing, ask:


- What does the command term require me to do?
- How many distinct points could the marks reasonably reward?
- Does the resource require a value, unit, location or comparison?
- Which example or case study directly supports my argument?
- How much time can I afford to spend here?
- Have I answered the exact question rather than the topic generally?


This checklist takes seconds. Those seconds can save marks that hours of extra revision may not recover.


### Misreading the command term


Maya’s first lost mark came from a question asking her to explain why vulnerability to a hazard varied between places. She described the differences clearly, but never explained the mechanisms behind them.


That distinction matters. A description identifies characteristics or patterns. An explanation connects a cause to an outcome. An evaluation weighs evidence and reaches a supported judgment. The precise expectations should always follow the terminology used in your course materials, but the larger lesson is simple: the verb determines the shape of the answer.


The official IB Geography specimen marking guidance rewards responses that are question-specific and aligned with the command term. It also distinguishes general knowledge from analysis supported by examples, statistics and case studies. In other words, knowing more cannot compensate for doing the wrong intellectual task.


Use this three-step routine:


1. Circle or underline the command term.
2. Translate it into an action, such as “give causes and consequences” or “consider strengths, limits and overall significance.”
3. Check your final sentence against that action.


The[IB exam command terms guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-exam-command-terms-list) is useful for building these distinctions. You can then open the[IB Geography Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-geography) , choose questions with different verbs and practise changing your answer structure accordingly.


A student trying to fit an enormous suitcase of geography knowledge through a doorway worth four marks


*Knowing everything is less useful when the question asks for four carefully selected marks.*


### Giving data without units or accurate evidence


Maya’s next error looked harmless. She correctly read a value of 42 from a graph, but the axis measured millions of people. Her answer said “42.” The number was present; the geographical evidence was not complete.


Whenever you use a graph, map or table, evidence usually needs context. That may include:


- the correct unit
- the named place or category
- an accurate value or defensible approximation
- the relevant year or period
- comparative language when the question asks for a contrast


A useful rule is **value plus unit plus meaning** . Instead of writing “42,” write “approximately 42 million people.” Instead of saying one region was “much higher,” use figures to establish the scale of the difference where the resource permits it.


Check axes carefully. Notice whether a scale begins at zero, whether percentages and percentage-point changes are being confused, and whether the legend changes how a map should be interpreted. If you calculate a difference, preserve the unit in the answer.


Case-study evidence can fail in a similar way. Merely naming a city, hazard or migration flow does not develop an argument. Explain what happened there and why that evidence supports the point you are making. The goal is not to recite an entire case study. It is to select the one detail that does the most work.


RevisionDojo’s[Geography self-study resource guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-ib-geography-resources-self-study) can help you combine Study Notes and Flashcards with application. Keep compact evidence cards containing the place, process, one or two useful figures, the date where relevant and the argument each example can support. AI Chat can then test whether you can use that evidence rather than merely recognise it.


### Writing everything you know instead of answering the question


Long answers often feel safe. They are not.


Maya saw a question about the effectiveness of one urban strategy and wrote everything she remembered about sustainable cities. The material was relevant to the topic, but much of it was not relevant to the claim she had been asked to assess.


This is a recurring lesson when students interpret[IB Geography examiner feedback](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-examiner-reports-what-they-reward) : specificity beats an information dump. Strong responses select knowledge, connect it to the wording of the question and sustain a line of reasoning.


For an extended response, plan around an argument rather than a list of facts:


- State a provisional judgment.
- Build each paragraph around a distinct reason.
- Add precise evidence.
- Explain how that evidence affects the argument.
- Consider a limitation, alternative scale or contrasting perspective.
- Return to the exact wording in the conclusion.


A useful paragraph test is: “If I removed the evidence, would the argument weaken?” If not, the example may be decorative. Another is: “If I changed the question slightly, could I submit the same paragraph?” If yes, the analysis is probably too generic.


### Losing control of time


Timing errors are unusually painful because they compound. Five unnecessary minutes on one response can leave an entire later section underdeveloped.


The fix begins before exam day. Allocate time in rough proportion to marks, while preserving a small checking buffer. Do not create a rigid universal formula without checking the structure and duration specified for your course and exam session. Instead, calculate a personal pace from the paper instructions supplied by your school and practise it repeatedly.


During the exam, use checkpoints. Write the time at which you intend to leave a major section. If that time arrives, complete the current thought and move on. A concise, complete attempt across the paper is generally more useful than polishing one answer while leaving another blank.


Timed practice should reproduce the choices that make exams difficult. No pausing. No checking Study Notes halfway through. No spending 12 minutes searching for the perfect case-study statistic. RevisionDojo’s guide to[IB Geography Mock Exams](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-geography-mock-exams-for-ib-an-in-depth-guide) recommends sorting errors into categories such as content, command term, evidence, structure and timing. That turns a disappointing mark into a diagnosis.


Use **Exam mode** for timed papers, then review the attempt with Grading tools. Record where time was lost and answer one similar Questionbank prompt under a tighter limit. The broader[IB practice and AI study tools guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/effective-ib-practice-resources-ai-study-tools) explains how Questionbank practice, Exam mode, Study Notes, Flashcards and AI feedback can form one cycle rather than separate revision activities.


### Turn each lost mark into a rule


A mistake log should not say only “lost two marks on rivers.” That describes the location of the problem, not its cause.


Write a rule you can reuse:


Mistake Reusable correction


Described instead of explaining Add a causal link using “because,” “therefore” or an equivalent mechanism


Copied a number without context Include value, unit, place and period where relevant


Named a case study without applying it Explain how the evidence supports the paragraph’s claim


Overwrote an early response Set section checkpoints and move when time expires


Produced a generic conclusion Answer the precise wording and state the extent of your judgment


This approach is more powerful than rereading because it changes future behaviour. The[guide to common IB exam mistakes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/common-ib-exam-mistakes) can help you identify patterns that extend beyond Geography, while the[IB Geography first-term guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-geography-first-term-struggles) shows how to move from knowing content to applying it under assessment conditions.


### Make easy marks less easy to lose


Maya’s hypothetical result did not require a dramatic rescue. She did not need another binder of notes. She needed clearer command-term habits, complete units, purposeful evidence and a clock she was willing to obey.


That is the encouraging part. These errors are trainable.


Practise short and extended responses in RevisionDojo’s Questionbank. Sit timed papers in Exam mode. Use Grading tools to separate knowledge gaps from execution errors, then return to Study Notes, Flashcards, Predicted Papers, Mock Exams, the Coursework Library or a RevisionDojo Tutor only where the diagnosis points. RevisionDojo brings those pieces together as the ultimate IB resource, but the principle remains simple: do not merely study more geography. Practise showing the examiner exactly what the question asks for.
